problem: Existing open-vocabulary navigation and mobile-manipulation memories (CLIP-Fields, VLMaps, ConceptGraphs, OK-Robot, etc.) assume a static environment. Many also need a pre-built map. They cannot delete stale objects or obstacles, and they always return a best match instead of reporting that a queried object is absent. So they fail when objects are moved by humans or by the robot itself.
motivation: In modular OVMM systems, a failure in the navigation/memory module propagates to the whole pipeline (the OK-Robot analysis). Real homes change constantly, so a static memory makes the robot go to where an object used to be. The authors attribute this to the lack of an online spatio-semantic memory that supports both adding and removing points, plus the lack of dynamic benchmarks for evaluating one.
key_idea: Keep an online sparse voxel point-cloud memory that stores, per voxel, a VLM feature, an observation count, the source image and a last-seen time. Add points from new posed RGB-D frames and delete points by view-frustum ray-casting. Answer open-vocabulary queries by retrieving the latest relevant image (via VLM features, an mLLM, or a hybrid of both) and verifying it with an open-vocabulary detector, so the system can abstain when the object is absent.
insight: Dynamic memory is what drives the real-world gain: OK-Robot's static map fails on 53.3% of trials because it cannot find moved objects, versus 6.7% for DynaMem, giving 70% vs 30% pick-and-drop success. The offline ablation shows the most important component is the OWL-v2 cross-check / abstention step (70.6% → 59.2% without it); point removal (70.6% vs 67.8% add-only) and similarity thresholding (66.8% without) help less. VLM features act like a bag of words (e.g., retrieving a blue bowl for 'red bowl'), while mLLM-QA is limited by context length and outdated images. The failures are complementary, so a hybrid that filters top-k=3 images with voxel features and then asks an mLLM scores best (74.5%).
method: Dynamic sparse voxel map: each voxel stores (x,y,z), observation count C, source image ID I, a CLIP/SigLIP feature f (count-weighted running average) and the latest observation time t. Features come from SAM-v2 object patches aggregated with the VLM.

Adding points: posed RGB-D frames are back-projected to global coordinates, clustered and assigned to voxels. Count and averaged feature are updated, and the voxel's image ID and timestamp are set to the latest observation.

Removing points via ray-casting: every existing voxel is projected into the current camera. It is deleted if it lies inside the image and its depth d satisfies 0 < d < min(2 m, D[h,w]+ε), i.e., it is in free space in front of the observed surface. Pixels beyond 2 m are ignored to limit depth noise.

Querying for localization: (a) VLM-feature mode takes the voxel with the highest text–feature dot product and retrieves its latest image, with DBSCAN clustering for top-k candidates. (b) mLLM-QA mode asks Gemini 1.5 Pro (up to 60 images; GPT-4o also tried) for the index of the last image containing the object, or 'None'. Images no longer referenced by any voxel are filtered out. (c) Hybrid mode sends the top-k VoxelMap images to the mLLM.
Abstention: OWL-v2 checks the candidate image for the query. If nothing is detected the system returns 'not found'; otherwise it returns the 3D location of the median mask pixel.

Navigation and exploration: voxels above 0.2 m are projected into a 2D obstacle map and those below as navigable; unknown cells are explorable. The robot does frontier exploration guided by sigmoid value maps over last-seen time (recency) and query–feature similarity (VLFM-style), which can be combined linearly. A* plans are executed closed-loop: the robot stops after 7 waypoints (~0.7–1 m), rescans, updates the map and replans.
Manipulation stack follows OK-Robot: AnyGrasp-based open-vocabulary grasping plus heuristic dropping, on a Hello Robot Stretch SE3.

numbers_note: No standard nav benchmarks are reported. The real-world lab results appear mainly in a failure-mode figure (Fig. failure); only the numbers quoted in the text are recorded here (OK-Robot baseline: 30% SR, 53.3% failures on moved objects; DynaMem 6.7% dynamic-nav failures). The benchmark name is an unexpanded LaTeX macro in the source (\BENCH{}), so 'DynaBench' is taken from the paper's name for it. Its environment count macro (\ENVNUM{}) is unexpanded; the text describes 3 robot-collected + 6 iPhone environments, which matches the abstract's 'nine offline scenes'. Other offline ablations: only adding points 67.8%, no OWL-v2 cross-check 59.2%, no similarity thresholding 66.8%, Gemini Pro 1.5 without voxelmap filtering 66.8%, human average 81.9%. The splits are not official; 'test' is used as a placeholder.
results: On a Stretch SE3 in 3 changing lab environments (30 pick-and-drop queries on non-stationary objects), DynaMem reaches 70% success with either VLM-feature or mLLM-QA querying, versus 30% for the static-memory OK-Robot baseline. OK-Robot fails on 53.3% of trials because it cannot find moved objects, compared with 6.7% for DynaMem. On the offline DynaBench, the hybrid query (voxel features pick the top-3 images, then Gemini 1.5 Pro chooses) scores 74.5%, above VLM-feature 70.6% and mLLM-QA 67.3%, against a human score of 81.9%. In 17 trials across two real apartments the hybrid system succeeded 9 times, with most failures due to navigation (4) and manipulation (3).
limitations: Small-scale evaluation: 30 lab queries and 17 home trials. The hybrid method was not run in the lab comparison, and there are no standard simulated benchmarks.

Localization failures remain. VLM features behave like a bag of words (wrong-color objects), and mLLM-QA is limited by context size (60 images) and outdated images. Removal only works for voxels within 2 m of the camera.
Many failures come from manipulation. The system also relies on a stable external SLAM and on heuristic thresholds (0.2 m ground cut-off, value-map sigmoid hyperparameters).
